title: History, staging and AIDS-defining illness
guide: First reported case in 1981 from an African patient, formerly lymphadenopathy-associated virus; CDC stages: 0 early HIV infection, 1 ≥500 cells/mm³, 2 200-499 cells/mm³ with CD4 14-28%, 3 <200 cells/mm³ or CD4 <14% with AIDS-defining conditions; AIDS-defining groups: malignancies (Burkitt's, EBV-mediated immunoblastic and primary CNS lymphoma, invasive cervical cancer, Kaposi's sarcoma), viral (CMV outside liver/spleen/nodes, HSV except zoster, JC virus PML), fungal (candidiasis of bronchi/trachea/lungs/oesophagus, extrapulmonary cryptococcosis, Pneumocystis jirovecii), parasitic (cerebral toxoplasmosis) and bacterial (MAC, MTB, Salmonella septicemia); category B non-defining conditions include vulvovaginal and oropharyngeal candidiasis, pelvic inflammatory disease, cervical dysplasia/carcinoma in situ, fever above 38.5 °C or diarrhoea beyond a month, ITP, herpes zoster, peripheral neuropathy and hairy leukoplakia; first Indian case in Chennai in 1986; Retroviridae with HTLV-1 (delta) causing adult T-cell lymphoma/leukemia and tropical spastic paraparesis, and lentiviruses HIV-1 and HIV-2 (less virulent, simian family, West African), envelope gp120/gp41, enzymes, capsid p17/p24, subtype C commonest and subtype B spread through blood and homosexuals.

title: Genes, transmission and replication
guide: Two copies of ssRNA; env codes gp120 spike and gp41 transmembrane pedicle protein, pol codes reverse transcriptase, integrase and protease, gag codes p17 matrix and p24 core (nucleocapsid) protein; non-structural genes Nef (negative effector downregulating host CD4), Vif, Rev, Tat, Vpr and Vpu/Vpx; sources with high concentration are blood, semen and vaginal fluid (as high as blood), pus from sores and CSF, while tears, saliva (with salivary lymphocyte inhibitory protein), urine and breast milk are low; transmission frequency sexual > parent to child > IV drug abuse > transfusion > needlestick, with the highest per-exposure risk being transfusion at 9,250 per 10,000; replication step 1 entry with gp120 change, CXCR4 (lymphocytes) or CCR5 (macrophages) co-receptor binding, gp41 change then fusion and uncoating (co-receptor blocker oral, fusion inhibitor subcutaneous), step 2 RNA to DNA, step 3 integration (oral integrase inhibitors), step 4 proliferation and release with protease cleavage (protease inhibitors); acute HIV infection after a 3-6 week incubation mimicking infectious mononucleosis with fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, diarrhoea and rash, no opportunistic infections, over 90% resolving and about 10% fulminant with meningoencephalitis, then establishment in GALT with long subclinical replication (clinical latency).

title: Course, diagnosis and opportunistic infections
guide: Pathogenesis: HIV-specific immune response, massive viraemia with wide dissemination to lymphoid organs, GALT seeding, chronic persistent infection with trapping of virus, partial immunologic control, then destruction of the immune system with accelerated replication, immune activation driven by cytokines and HIV envelope-mediated aberrant cell signalling and rapid CD4 T-cell turnover; untreated course runs primary infection with or without acute HIV syndrome, dissemination and lymphoid seeding, clinical latency, constitutional symptoms with skin and mucous-membrane defects and systemic deficiency, opportunistic disease and death; graph shows CD4 count, HIV RNA copies and anti-HIV antibody over weeks then years; HIV RNA detectable around day 10 (1-2 weeks), p24 by day 16 (2-3 weeks) and antibody last; testing uses the 4th-generation HIV-1/HIV-2 antigen/antibody combination immunoassay, negative means no HIV, positive goes to the HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay, and if no antibodies are detected HIV-1 NAT decides between acute HIV-1 infection and a negative result; opportunistic infections by CD4: lymphadenopathy/thrombocytopenia near 600, Kaposi's sarcoma at any count, oral hairy leukoplakia/TB, mucocutaneous herpes, cryptosporidiosis and microsporidiosis near 300, Pneumocystis, miliary TB and oesophageal candidiasis near 200, cerebral toxoplasmosis and cryptococcal meningitis near 100, primary CNS lymphoma at 50-100, and HIV-associated dementia, PML, CMV retinitis and MAC at the lowest counts.

title: Treatment: drugs, regimens and prophylaxis
guide: CMV retinitis has the pizza-pie fundus; MAC presents with disseminated disease — fever, night sweats, weight loss and lymphadenopathy with rare pulmonary involvement — at an average CD4 below 10, treated with clarithromycin plus ethambutol and prevented with azithromycin when CD4 falls below 50; all HIV must be treated; drug classes are CD4 receptor inhibitors (ibalizumab IV), co-receptor inhibitors (maraviroc oral), fusion inhibitors (enfuvirtide subcutaneous), integrase inhibitors (dolutegravir, raltegravir), protease inhibitors (ritonavir, nelfinavir, atazanavir) and reverse-transcriptase inhibitors — NRTIs abacavir, lamivudine and emtricitabine, NNRTIs nevirapine, efavirenz and delavirdine, and the nucleotide RTI tenofovir disoproxil; preferred three-drug combination is TED (tenofovir 300 mg, emtricitabine 200 mg, dolutegravir 50 mg, all once daily) with the NACO/TLD regimen substituting lamivudine 300 mg for emtricitabine; post-needlestick prophylaxis uses the TED regimen for 4 weeks and is optimally effective within 72 hours; tenofovir carries bone toxicity.
